name: Keeping Seniors on Track Over the Summer
title: Keeping Seniors on Track Over the Summer
answer: Keeping seniors on track over the summer means using outreach, such as texts and peer or chatbot support, to help graduating students complete enrollment tasks after counselors are no longer in regular contact. It matters because students with the least support are most at risk of missing steps like deposits, final transcripts, and orientation, and this outreach can raise college enrollment. The support should be monitored by a person and should stop once a student enrolls or chooses another path.

sections.body: After graduation, seniors often lose their usual access to counselors at the exact time they must handle deposits, final transcripts, and orientation sign-up. Students with the least support are hit hardest by this summer gap, which the text calls summer melt. The idea is to keep a light but reliable line of contact open through texting platforms and outreach, so questions get answered and reminders arrive before deadlines pass. This solves a coordination problem, not an academic one, because the student may already be admitted but still needs help completing the steps to actually enroll. The support matters most for those with the least, especially students who have no one at home who has been through the process.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: For graduating seniors, schools can use texting platforms to stay in touch across the summer. A counselor or another staff member should watch replies and answer questions the tool cannot handle. The outreach can include reminders and quick responses, and the text describes peer mentors and chatbot tools as ways to provide that contact. The messages should continue only until a student has enrolled or chosen a different path. Families should be told that the outreach is happening and should be given a way to opt out.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text reports an early trial in which personalized text messages and outreach from peer mentors over the summer raised college enrollment, especially for students with less access to counseling (Castleman & Page, 2015). It also says the chatbot trial described at the start of the chapter found similar effects with an AI tool (Page & Gehlbach, 2017). A later trial with 4,442 admitted students found that chatbot outreach helped most with financial aid steps and that the benefits were concentrated among first generation college students (Nurshatayeva et al., 2021). The text does not give a separate evidence label beyond these trial findings.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The text sets limits on how this outreach should run. A person, such as a counselor or staff member, must monitor replies and answer questions that the tool cannot. The messages should end when students have enrolled or chosen another path, so the contact does not continue past its purpose. Families should know the outreach is happening and should have a clear way to opt out. Decisions about monitoring, answering, and stopping the messages stay with school staff rather than the tool.
